Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider a plane lamina that occupies the region [MATH: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2] of mass [MATH: M] where the center of mass is at [MATH: \left(\bar{x},\bar{y}\right).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e6d0f787d87ad36b4fe86adb9374f8c5]

Content:
We know that the lamina has some moment of inertia [MATH: I_M] about the line [MATH: l_M] that passes through the center of mass and is perpendicular to the lamina.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4932ea929465c809ec3e54668d196905]

Content:
Now, if [MATH: l] is a line parallel to [MATH: l_M,] then the lamina also has moment of inertia about [MATH: l,] say [MATH: I_l.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9894693079df419a00fa75b3a7ce48da]

Content:
Given the value of [MATH: I_M,] we can find [MATH: I_l] using the parallel axis theorem, which states that

Content:
[MATH: I_l = I_M + d^2M,]

Content:
where [MATH: d] is the distance between the lines.

Content:
The term [MATH: d^2M] is the moment of inertia about [MATH: l] of the lamina when its entire mass is concentrated at the center of mass.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/586d448bbcaa36ad577144dd8f7b6a53]

Content:
So, our interpretation of the parallel axis theorem is the following:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{\text{moment of inertia of }D \ \text{about a parallel line }l}_{I_l}
\:=\:
\underbrace{\text{moment of inertia of }D \ \text{about the center of mass}}_{I_M}
\:+\:
\underbrace{\text{moment of inertia of point mass }M \ \text{about the parallel line } l}_{d^2M}]

Content:
Finally, since [MATH: d^2M] is always positive, we have [MATH: I_M \leq I_l] for any line [MATH: l] perpendicular to the lamina. In other words, the moment of inertia about the line through its center of mass is the smallest moment of inertia about any line in that direction.

The distance between the line through the center of mass [MATH: (0,1)] and the line through the point [MATH: (2,1)] is

[MATH: d|= sqrt((2 − 0)^{2} + (1 − 1)^{2}); = sqrt(4 + 0); = sqrt(4); = 2.]
